prize_parts.citation: For transforming the measurement of intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data, and for identifying how childhood environment and place causally shape economic opportunity.

statement.case_for: B002 pairs new data with a framework and credible designs, which is the combination I think the prize rewards. Linking population-scale administrative records made intergenerational mobility observable at fine geographic resolution. The same work then used quasi-experimental variation, such as childhood exposure and movers designs, to separate causal place effects from sorting. This is more than data discovery, because the data are tied to explanatory designs and to welfare-relevant policy questions. The impact on research, on how administrative data are used in public and labour economics, and on public debate is large. It was also the most widely supported entry in the openings, but I do not treat that as evidence of merit. My case rests on the contribution itself, which is well defined and attributable to three people. The final trio matches what nearly every colleague who ranked it proposed, with Chetty, Hendren and Friedman as the closest collaborators on the mobility and place-effects papers.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. Most core results date from about 2014 to 2022, and the long-run causal interpretation of neighbourhood and exposure effects is still being tested and debated. This is a large team-based programme, so a three-name cap is somewhat arbitrary. It leaves out Katz, whose Moving to Opportunity work is an important input, and it concentrates credit in a way that may understate other collaborators. If the committee judges that a decade is too short to confirm the causal claims, B002 should wait. B024 is the natural fallback, since it has a longer record of replication and debate.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B002 sixth and calls it possibly premature relative to other candidates. He notes that replication and long-term follow-up are still accumulating, that credit is hard to divide among many co-authors, and that the causal reading of neighbourhood effects is contested.
responses.response: I take the timing concern seriously and it is the main reason I do not treat B002 as a certainty. I still think it is weaker as an objection than it first looks. Much of the core mobility and exposure evidence has been replicated or extended with other administrative datasets, and the findings do not rest on one dataset or specification. The unresolved questions concern the size and interpretation of specific causal place effects, not the existence of the measurement advance or the design approach. The attribution worry also seems less severe here than in the macro entries. The mobility and place-effects papers have identifiable lead authors, so a three-person prize is defensible. I would accept that the committee must be explicit in the citation about what is established, namely the measurement and the exposure-based designs, and avoid overclaiming on long-run policy conclusions.

responses.point: Teorell ranks the political-economics entry (B027) first. He argues it created a field and combines rigorous theory with empirical tests, is mature and has no timing concern. He also acknowledges that the cross-country identification of electoral-rule effects is less clean than the theory.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on field-creating influence, and B027 is my alternative if the committee wants a longer track record than B002 offers. My difference with Teorell is how much weight to give identification. His own admission that the electoral-rule findings rest on cross-country identification that is less clean than the theory matters under common criteria. In B002 the empirical claims come from designs that exploit within-family and mover variation, so they can be evaluated directly. I also see a boundary problem in B027. Its attribution has to be separated from the 2024 institutions prize, and the credit between theory and cross-country evidence is hard to divide. I do not think that makes B027 unqualified, but it keeps me from ranking it above B002.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first and describes the contribution as turning mobility into a measurable, place-specific object. He assigns Hendren to causal place effects and welfare measurement, and Friedman to data construction and tax-record work, and he leaves Katz off to respect the cap.
responses.response: I agree with this division and with the trio. I want to qualify one point. I would not describe Friedman's role as only data construction, since the data work is bound up with the conceptual and design choices that make the mobility estimates interpretable. So I read the three names as complementary on measurement, causal design and welfare interpretation, rather than as one leader and two assistants. On Boppart's worry about credit concentrating in Chetty, I think the citation should be written around the discovery, meaning mobility measurement and place effects, and not around a person or the broader oeuvre. That protects the attribution and lets Katz's earlier work be acknowledged in the citation context without adding a fourth name.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 seventh and calls it less mature than the other candidates. He worries that the findings may prove data-driven rather than foundational, and that Katz and the breadth of the credited team make a different split possible.
responses.response: The risk that a high-profile empirical programme proves to be data-driven rather than foundational is real, and I cannot dismiss it. My response is that the lasting part appears to be methodological and conceptual: the use of population administrative data as a standard, and the designs for separating place effects from selection. Both already shape other work, including studies using Swedish and other national registers, which I know from my own field. Even if specific point estimates move, that part will remain. I recognise that the Katz question is a closer call than my ranking suggests, and I would not object to a configuration that credited him if the committee prefers that split.

uncertainties: How much further replication of the causal neighbourhood and exposure effects the committee wants before treating the result as settled.
Whether Katz should be one of the three names for B002 instead of one of the closest collaborators, and how that interacts with his credit in B024.
Whether B024 or B027 is the better fallback, given the persistence debate over trade-shock effects and the identification and overlap concerns about political economics.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied openings, and I have not independently verified citations or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My work in labour economics, crime and administrative-data quasi-experiments is close to B002 and B024, and I disclose that closeness without adjudicating it.
